How to use this guide

এই গাইড কীভাবে ব্যবহার করবেন

This guide walks you through every clause of AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 3 (SS 3). Each chapter starts from what the standard actually says, then adds the reasoning AAOIFI gives in its Appendix (B), then shows how other authorities and Bangladeshi banks deal with the same issue. Worked examples use Bangladeshi Taka (BDT).

The standard's own text is paraphrased. Only short phrases are quoted. Every point carries a chip showing the clause number and the page of the source PDF, for example SS 3 · 2/1/2 · p. 88 , so you can check it against the original.

Four kinds of authority — keep them apart

KindWhat it isExample in this topic
1. Shari'ah evidenceQur'an and authentic Sunnah. Binding in itself."Delay by a person of means is injustice" (Bukhari 2287).
2. Juristic opinionHow a school or scholar reads the evidence. Can differ.Maliki jurists allowing a binding promise to donate (iltizam bi al-tabarru').
3. StandardsCollective rulings issued by bodies such as AAOIFI and IIFA. Binding where adopted.SS 3 clause 2/1/2: no compensation for late payment.
4. RegulationCentral bank rules. Legally binding in that country.Bangladesh Bank 2026 credit-card guideline: late-payment amount goes to a segregated charity account.
STUDY TIP

When you answer an exam question, say which of the four you are citing. "AAOIFI says…" is a standard; "the Prophet (peace be upon him) said…" is evidence; "Bangladesh Bank requires…" is regulation. Mixing them up is the most common mistake.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

কুরআন-হাদিস হলো মূল দলিল। ফকিহদের ব্যাখ্যা হলো মতামত। AAOIFI বা ফিকহ একাডেমির সিদ্ধান্ত হলো স্ট্যান্ডার্ড। আর বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংকের সার্কুলার হলো আইনগত নিয়ম। উত্তর লেখার সময় এই চারটিকে আলাদা করে উল্লেখ করুন।

1. Purpose, scope and map of the standard

অধ্যায় ১: উদ্দেশ্য, পরিধি ও স্ট্যান্ডার্ডের মানচিত্র

1.1 What problem does SS 3 solve?

A conventional bank has an easy answer when a borrower pays late: it charges more interest. An Islamic bank cannot do this, because any increase in a debt in return for more time is riba. So what can an Islamic financial institution (IFI) do when a customer who can pay simply will not pay? SS 3 answers that question. It lists what is forbidden, and it gives the IFI a toolkit of lawful ways to protect itself.

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · Preface · p. 87

The standard explains the Shari'ah rulings for IFI transactions where solvent debtors or guarantors delay settling what they owe, and where contractors are late in performing, which triggers a penalty clause in their contract. A footnote says "Institution" means Islamic financial institutions, including Islamic banks.

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 1 · p. 88

Covered: (i) default by a solvent debtor; (ii) default by a solvent guarantor; (iii) a contractor or concessionaire who finishes late and so becomes a debtor under a penalty clause. Not covered: debtors who are insolvent or bankrupt, and debtors who delay for a reason the Shari'ah accepts.

Figure 1. Who is a "procrastinating debtor"? Only the left branch falls inside SS 3.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

"মুমাতিল" বা টালবাহানাকারী দেনাদার হলো সেই ব্যক্তি, যার পরিশোধের সামর্থ্য আছে, তবুও বৈধ কোনো কারণ ছাড়াই কিস্তি বা দেনা পরিশোধে দেরি করে। যিনি সত্যিই অক্ষম (মু'সির), তাঁর বিষয় এই স্ট্যান্ডার্ডের আওতায় পড়ে না; কুরআনের নির্দেশ অনুযায়ী তাঁকে সচ্ছল হওয়া পর্যন্ত সময় দিতে হবে। আবার কেউ যদি শরিয়াহসম্মত কারণে দেরি করেন, যেমন পণ্যে ত্রুটি নিয়ে প্রকৃত বিরোধ, তিনিও এর বাইরে।

1.3 Current status of SS 3

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH
  • The copy studied here is the revised version. The Shari'ah Standards Review Committee reviewed it in November 2011, and the Shari'ah Board approved the amendments at meeting No. 38 in June 2014 (App. A, p. 93).
  • AAOIFI's own standard page still lists SS 3 – Procrastinating Debtor, with the same scope wording; the full text is behind member access (cis.aaoifi.com). In searches up to November 2026 we found no newer exposure draft or replacement of SS 3. AAOIFI's recent announcements concern accounting and governance standards. Check AAOIFI's site before relying on this.
  • Pakistan: the State Bank of Pakistan adopted SS 3 (under the title "Default in Payment by a Debtor") by IBD Circular No. 01 of 2010, dated 12 January 2010, with one amendment (see Chapter 7).
  • Bangladesh: Bangladesh Bank has not formally adopted AAOIFI SS 3 as a regulation. Its 2026 Islamic credit card guideline, however, follows the same charity-undertaking model (Chapter 7).
STUDY TIP

Remember SS 3 as "1 prohibition, 2 'nos', 8 tools": procrastination is haram (1); no contractual compensation and no court-awarded compensation (2 nos); and eight lawful tools: costs, collateral sale, acceleration, repossession, charity undertaking, guarantor, blacklist, set-off.

2. Evidence and key terms

অধ্যায় ২: শরিয়াহ দলিল ও মূল পরিভাষা

2.1 Evidence from the Qur'an and Sunnah

Hadith numbers below follow the sunnah.com numbering. AAOIFI's Appendix (B) cites older printed editions by volume and page, so its numbers look different.

EVIDENCE 1 · DELAY BY THE ABLE IS INJUSTICE

مَطْلُ الْغَنِيِّ ظُلْمٌ

Meaning: When a person who has the means delays paying, that is injustice (zulm). Source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2287; Sahih Muslim 1564 (Abu Hurayrah). Grade: sahih (agreed upon). Relevance: The basis of 2/1/1. The word ghani (person of means) limits the ruling to the solvent debtor.

EVIDENCE 2 · HIS HONOUR AND PUNISHMENT BECOME LAWFUL

لَيُّ الْوَاجِدِ يُحِلُّ عِرْضَهُ وَعُقُوبَتَهُ

Meaning: Delay by one who has the means makes it lawful to speak against him and to punish him. Source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3628 (al-Sharid); also al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah; al-Bukhari mentions it without a full chain (mu'allaq). Grade: hasan (al-Albani). Relevance: The basis of the non-material sanctions in 2/4 (blacklisting, warning others). Note that "punishment" here was understood by jurists as imprisonment or similar by a judge, not a money charge that the creditor keeps.

EVIDENCE 3 · GRACE FOR THE ONE IN HARDSHIP

وَإِن كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ فَنَظِرَةٌ إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ

Meaning: If the debtor is in hardship, give him time until things become easier. Source: Qur'an, al-Baqarah 2:280. Relevance: Explains why insolvent debtors are outside SS 3 (clause 1). AAOIFI states the same point at App. B, p. 94.

EVIDENCE 4 · TRADE IS LAWFUL, RIBA IS NOT

وَأَحَلَّ اللَّهُ الْبَيْعَ وَحَرَّمَ الرِّبَا

Meaning: Allah has made trade lawful and riba unlawful. Source: Qur'an 2:275; see also 2:278–279. Relevance: Any extra amount charged for extra time on a debt is the riba of the pre-Islamic era ("pay now or increase"), which App. B (p. 95) describes. This is why 2/1/2 bans late-payment compensation.

EVIDENCE 5 · MUSLIMS ARE BOUND BY THEIR CONDITIONS

الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى شُرُوطِهِمْ إِلَّا شَرْطًا حَرَّمَ حَلَالًا أَوْ أَحَلَّ حَرَامًا

Meaning: Muslims are held to their conditions, except a condition that makes the lawful unlawful or the unlawful lawful. Source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1352 (Tirmidhi: hasan sahih); shorter wording in Abi Dawud 3594. Grade note: Tirmidhi's chain runs through Kathir ibn 'Abdullah al-Muzani, whom many hadith critics considered weak; scholars accept the hadith as hasan through its several routes. Treat it as acceptable, but know the debate. Relevance: Used three ways in App. B: the late-payment condition is void (it makes riba lawful); penalty clauses in construction are valid (they do not); set-off and sequence-of-demand conditions are binding.

EVIDENCE 6 · GIVE EVERYONE HIS DUE

أَعْطِ كُلَّ ذِي حَقٍّ حَقَّهُ

Meaning: Give each one who has a right his right. Source: Words of Salman al-Farisi to Abu al-Darda', which the Prophet (peace be upon him) confirmed: Sahih al-Bukhari 1968; also Tirmidhi 2413. Grade: sahih. (SS 3 cites only Tirmidhi.) Relevance: General duty to settle debts on time.

EVIDENCE 7 · THE SELLER WHO FINDS HIS GOODS WITH A BANKRUPT

مَنْ أَدْرَكَ مَالَهُ بِعَيْنِهِ عِنْدَ رَجُلٍ قَدْ أَفْلَسَ فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ

Meaning: Whoever finds his very property with a man who has gone bankrupt has more right to it than anyone else. Source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2402; Sahih Muslim 1559 (Abu Hurayrah). Grade: sahih. Relevance: The basis of 2/1/7 (Murabahah seller may take the asset back).

EVIDENCE 8 · SURETYSHIP

وَلِمَن جَاءَ بِهِ حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ وَأَنَا بِهِ زَعِيمٌ

Meaning: "Whoever brings it will have a camel's load, and I guarantee it." Source: Qur'an, Yusuf 12:72; and Abu Qatadah guaranteeing a dead man's debt so that the Prophet (peace be upon him) would pray over him: Bukhari 2289 (three dinars), Abi Dawud 3343 (two dinars, from Jabir). Relevance: The basis of 2/2. SS 3 quotes the "two dinars" wording, which matches the Jabir version, not Bukhari's.

EVIDENCE 9 · THE BEST OF YOU ARE BEST IN REPAYING

إِنَّ خِيَارَكُمْ أَحْسَنُكُمْ قَضَاءً

Meaning: The best of you are those who repay in the best way. Source: Bukhari 2305; Muslim 1601 (Abu Hurayrah); and the Prophet (peace be upon him) repaying a better camel: Muslim 1600. Also Qur'an 9:91: "there is no blame on those who do good". Relevance: The basis of 2/5/2: an extra amount is allowed only if it is the debtor's free gift, not a condition or custom.

EVIDENCE 10 · TAKE WHAT IS ENOUGH, FAIRLY

خُذِي مَا يَكْفِيكِ وَوَلَدَكِ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ

Meaning: Take what is sufficient for you and your child, in a fair way. Source: Said to Hind, wife of Abu Sufyan: Bukhari 5364; Muslim 1714. Grade: sahih. Relevance: Basis of the creditor's right to recover what is owed from the debtor's property in its hands (al-zafar), and so of set-off in 2/5/3.

WEAK OR MISATTRIBUTED — DO NOT CITE AS HADITH

"Every loan that brings a benefit is riba" ( )(كُلُّ قَرْضٍ جَرَّ نَفْعًا فَهُوَ رِبًا)is widely quoted, but its

chains to the Prophet (peace be upon him) are weak. It is a juristic maxim supported by reports from Companions, not a sahih hadith. SS 3 does not rely on it; it speaks only of reports from "many companions" (App. B, p. 95).

2.2 Key-term cards

1. Procrastination / default المُمَاطَلَة · المَطْل

Transliteration: mutl; mumatalah

Literal: stretching out, dragging

Technical: Delay in settling an obligation that is due, without a legitimate reason (App. C, p. 101).

Plain English: Stalling on a payment you could make.

বাংলা টালবাহানা; সামর্থ্য থাকা সত্ত্বেও পরিশোধে গড়িমসি।

Example: A trader with BDT 30 lakh in stock keeps postponing a BDT 2 lakh instalment.

2. Procrastinating debtorالمَدِينُ المُمَاطِل

Transliteration: al-madin al-mumatil

Literal: the stalling debtor

Technical: A solvent debtor who refuses to pay a due debt without a legitimate reason after a normal demand (App. C, p. 101).

Plain English: Can pay, was asked, still won't.

বাংলা সামর্থ্যবান অথচ পরিশোধে বিলম্বকারী দেনাদার।

Example: A salaried customer with BDT 4 lakh in a deposit account ignores two reminder letters.

3. Insolvent debtor المَدِينُ المُعْسِر

Transliteration: al-madin al-mu'sir

Literal: the one in hardship

Technical: A debtor whose assets do not allow payment; must be given time (Qur'an 2:280). Outside SS 3.

Plain English: Wants to pay, can't.

বাংলা অসচ্ছল বা অক্ষম দেনাদার, যাকে সময় দিতে হবে।

Example: A farmer whose crop was destroyed by flood.

4. Riba الرِّبَا

Transliteration: riba

Literal: increase, growth

Technical: Here, riba al-duyun: any increase on a debt in return for time, agreed or demanded.

Plain English: Charging for time on money owed.

বাংলা সুদ; দেনার ওপর সময়ের বিনিময়ে অতিরিক্ত।

Example: "2% per month on overdue amounts, credited to bank income."

5. Compensation التَّعْوِيض

Transliteration: ta'wid (Malaysia: ta'widh)

Literal: making good, replacing

Technical: Money paid to cover the creditor's loss. Banned by SS 3 for late payment of a debt, whether for opportunity loss or currency loss (2/1/2).

Plain English: "Pay us for what we lost while you were late."

বাংলা ক্ষতিপূরণ।

Example: Asking for 9% p.a. on the overdue sum because "that is our profit rate".

6. Penalty clause الشَّرْطُ الجَزَائِي

Transliteration: al-shart al-jaza'i

Literal: the sanction condition

Technical: A pre-agreed amount due to the obligee if the obligor delays performance (App. C, p. 101). Allowed for non-debt obligations (2/3).

Plain English: Liquidated damages for late work.

বাংলা জরিমানার শর্ত; কাজ দেরিতে হলে পূর্বনির্ধারিত অর্থ।

Example: BDT 50,000 per week of delay in handing over a building.

7. Undertaking to donate الالْتِزَامُ بِالتَّبَرُّع

Transliteration: iltizam bi al-tabarru'

Literal: binding oneself to give

Technical: The debtor's promise, in the contract, to donate an amount or percentage to charity through the IFI if he procrastinates (2/1/8). Maliki basis.

Plain English: A "late-fee" that goes to charity, never to the bank.

বাংলা দান করার অঙ্গীকার।

Example: BDT 1,000 per missed instalment paid into the bank's charity account.

8. Guarantor / surety الكَفِيل · الضَّامِن

Transliteration: kafil; damin (also za'im)

Literal: one who takes on, sponsor

Technical: One who adds his liability to the debtor's; the creditor may claim from either unless sequence was stipulated (2/2).

Plain English: The person who said "if he doesn't pay, I will".

বাংলা জামিনদার।

Example: A father guaranteeing his son's car financing.

9. Pledge / collateralالرَّهْن

Transliteration: rahn

Literal: holding, confinement

Technical: An asset held as security; the creditor may have it sold to settle the debt, with or without a court, if the debtor gave a mandate (2/1/5).

Plain English: Security you can sell.

বাংলা বন্ধক বা জামানত।

Example: A mortgaged flat in Mirpur.

10. Acceleration of instalmentsحُلُولُ الأَقْسَاط

Transliteration: hulul al-aqsat

Literal: the instalments falling due

Technical: A condition that all remaining instalments become payable when the debtor misses one (2/1/6). The total does not increase.

Plain English: "Miss one, owe all now."

বাংলা সকল কিস্তি একসাথে পরিশোধযোগ্য হওয়া।

Example: 15 remaining instalments of BDT 50,000 all become due at once.

11. Set-off المُقَاصَّة

Transliteration: muqassah

Literal: mutual cutting-off

Technical: Settling the overdue debt from the customer's balances with the IFI, as stipulated (2/5/3). See also AAOIFI SS 4.

Plain English: The bank pays itself from your account.

বাংলা সমন্বয়; গ্রাহকের হিসাব থেকে পাওনা কেটে নেওয়া।

Example: BDT 80,000 taken from a Mudarabah savings account.

12. Good repayment حُسْنُ القَضَاء

Transliteration: husn al-qada'

Literal: fine settlement

Technical: A voluntary extra on repayment, with no condition, promise or custom (2/5/2).

Plain English: A genuine thank-you, not a fee.

বাংলা উত্তমভাবে পরিশোধ; স্বেচ্ছায় কিছু বেশি দেওয়া।

Example: A customer adds BDT 2,000 on his own; no form or policy suggested it.

2.3 Which contract governs which relationship?

STUDY TIP

The single question that decides almost every case: "Is the late obligation a debt (dayn)?" If yes, no penalty that benefits the creditor. If it is work or delivery of a non-debt thing, a penalty clause is allowed.

3. Default by the debtor: the core prohibition

অধ্যায় ৩: দেনাদারের খেলাপ — মূল নিষেধাজ্ঞা (২/১/১–২/১/৪, ২/৬)

3.1 Procrastination is haram

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/1 · p. 88

When a debtor who is able to pay fails to pay, that default is haram (prohibited).

Characteristics. Three things must be present together: (1) a debt that is due; (2) the debtor is able to pay; (3) there is no legitimate reason for delay.

Reasoning from the standard. App. B (p. 94) relies on Evidences 1, 2 and 6 (Chapter 2) and reports that scholars agree such a debtor may be punished, while an insolvent debtor must be given time.

Juristic logic. The debt is the creditor's property in the debtor's hands. Keeping it back without excuse is a form of taking another's property, which is zulm. That is why the sin is on the debtor, not merely a contract breach.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

সামর্থ্য থাকা সত্ত্বেও দেনা পরিশোধে দেরি করা শুধু চুক্তিভঙ্গ নয়, এটি গুনাহ ও জুলুম। কারণ পাওনাদারের অর্থ দেনাদার অন্যায়ভাবে আটকে রাখছে। তবে এই হারাম হওয়ার বিধান কেবল সামর্থ্যবান দেনাদারের জন্য।

3.2 No compensation for late payment — in the contract or in court

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/2 · p. 88

The contract may not stipulate financial compensation for delay, in cash or in kind, whether the amount is fixed in advance or not. The ban covers compensation for lost income (opportunity loss) and for loss due to a fall in the value of the currency of the debt.

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/3 · p. 88

The creditor may not go to court to demand compensation from the defaulting debtor, in cash or in kind, for the delay.

Reasoning from the standard (App. B, p. 95). Such a condition is riba and void, whether agreed at the start or at maturity. Three supports are given: the hadith on conditions (Evidence 5); the pre-Islamic practice where lenders asked "will you pay now or pay more for more time?"; and IIFA Resolution 51, which forbids stipulating compensation for delay. A court order would have the same effect as a contract clause, so neither route is allowed.

Juristic logic. The test is substance, not name. Calling the charge "compensation", "ta'widh", "service fee" or "delay fee" does not change what it is: more money for more time on a debt, kept by the creditor. The currency-loss point closes a loophole: indexing a debt to inflation would also increase it for time.

Figure 2. The same delay, two outcomes. Only the amount of the debt and genuine costs may reach the creditor.

EXAMPLE · MURABAHAH IN DHAKA

An Islamic bank sells machinery to Karim Traders on Murabahah for BDT 12,00,000, payable in 24 monthly instalments of BDT 50,000. Karim misses 3 instalments (BDT 1,50,000) though his shop is doing well.

  • Bank may not add 2% per month (BDT 3,000 a month, BDT 9,000 for three months) to its income.
  • Bank may not claim "our cost of funds was 9% p.a., so pay us BDT 3,375" (1,50,000 × 9% × 3/12).
  • Bank may not claim the Taka lost 5% against the dollar, so Karim owes BDT 7,500 more.
  • Bank may claim the BDT 1,50,000 and actual legal costs (3.3 below).
NON-COMPLIANCE
  • A schedule of charges that says "compensation at x% on overdue amount" and books it as income.
  • Rescheduling an overdue Murabahah by raising the total price for the extra time.
  • Asking a court or arbitrator to award "damages for delay" on a financing debt.
  • Linking the overdue amount to an inflation index, gold or USD to "protect value".
ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · IIFA

IIFA Resolution 51 (2/6) (Jeddah, March 1990) says that if a buyer delays instalments, no increase may be added to the debt, whether agreed in advance or demanded later, as this is riba; and even a solvent delaying debtor may not be charged compensation. Resolution 133 (7/14) (Doha, January 2003) reaffirms this and asks banks to study the root causes of arrears and develop new recovery mechanisms.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · THE MINORITY VIEW

Some contemporary scholars (for example Shaykh Mustafa al-Zarqa and Shaykh al-Siddiq al-Darir) argued for compensation of the creditor's actual proven loss from a wilful defaulter. AAOIFI and IIFA rejected this. Malaysia's regulator partly follows a version of it (Chapter 7). Practical effect: under AAOIFI, an IFI's only financial "pressure" that is not a cost recovery is the charity undertaking, which gives the bank no income.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

দেরিতে পরিশোধের জন্য ব্যাংক নিজের আয় হিসেবে কোনো অতিরিক্ত টাকা নিতে পারবে না — চুক্তিতে শর্ত দিয়েও না, আদালতে মামলা করেও না। নাম "ক্ষতিপূরণ" রাখলেও বাস্তবে এটি সময়ের বিনিময়ে বাড়তি অর্থ, অর্থাৎ সুদ। মুদ্রার মান কমে যাওয়ার অজুহাতেও বাড়তি নেওয়া যাবে না।

3.3 Legal and recovery costs

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/4 · p. 88

The procrastinating debtor bears the legal and other expenses the creditor incurs to recover the debt.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 96): the debtor caused the costs. AAOIFI cites Ibn Taymiyyah and later Hanbali authorities.

Juristic logic. This is not compensation for time; it is reimbursement of actual money spent because of the default. The amount must be real and documented, not a fixed percentage of the debt.

EXAMPLE

The bank pays a lawyer BDT 15,000 and court fees of BDT 3,500 to recover Karim's BDT 1,50,000. Karim may be charged BDT 18,500 (15,000 + 3,500). A flat "recovery fee of 5% of overdue" (BDT 7,500) would not qualify, because it is not tied to actual cost.

NON-COMPLIANCE

Charging in-house staff time or a fixed "collection fee" that is in reality a disguised late charge. The Bangladesh Bank 2026 credit-card guideline makes the same point: collection costs may be recovered only to the extent actually paid to external agents.

3.4 When is default established?

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/6 · p. 90

Default is established when, after a normal demand for payment, a debtor who has not proved insolvency fails to pay on the due date.

Juristic logic. Two points matter. First, there must be a normal demand (a reminder, a notice). Second, the burden of proof is on the debtor to show insolvency; the bank does not have to prove that he is rich.

STUDY TIP

Learn the definition as "Due + Demand + No proof of hardship = Default". Exams often give a case with no demand letter: then default is not yet established under 2/6.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

খেলাপ প্রমাণিত হয় তখন, যখন নির্ধারিত তারিখ পেরিয়ে যায়, ব্যাংক স্বাভাবিকভাবে পরিশোধ চায়, আর দেনাদার নিজের অক্ষমতা প্রমাণ করতে পারেন না। অক্ষমতা প্রমাণের দায়িত্ব দেনাদারের।

4. Lawful recovery tools

অধ্যায় ৪: পাওনা আদায়ের বৈধ উপায় (২/১/৫–২/১/৮, ২/৫/৩)

Having closed the door on late-payment compensation, SS 3 opens several other doors. None of them increases the debt for the creditor's benefit.

Figure 3. Eight lawful tools in SS 3, with clause numbers.

4.1 Selling the collateral

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/5 · pp. 88–89

The creditor may apply for the sale of an asset mortgaged as security, to settle the debt. It may also stipulate that the debtor gives it a mandate (agency) to sell the mortgaged asset without going to court.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 96): selling is already permissible for the creditor; a mandate simply speeds things up. The creditor may also seek sale of the debtor's other property in its possession.

Juristic logic. The bank sells as the debtor's agent. So it must sell at a fair price, take only what is owed (debt plus actual costs) and return any surplus to the debtor.

EXAMPLE

A flat pledged for a BDT 40 lakh outstanding balance is sold for BDT 52 lakh. Sale costs are BDT 1.2 lakh. The bank keeps BDT 41.2 lakh (40 + 1.2) and must pay the remaining BDT 10.8 lakh (52 − 41.2) to the customer.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · SBP AMENDMENT

When the State Bank of Pakistan adopted SS 3, it added to this sub-clause the words "on giving the debtor reasonable notice of sale" (SBP Compendium). So in Pakistan the mandate to sell can only be used after reasonable notice. In Bangladesh, sale of mortgaged property is also governed by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 and the Transfer of Property Act, which the SSC must check.

4.2 Accelerating all instalments

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/6 · p. 89

Unless the failure was caused by force majeure, the contract may say that all outstanding instalments become due when the procrastinating debtor fails to pay one. It is preferable to apply this only after notifying the debtor and allowing a reasonable time. (Cross-reference: SS 5 on Guarantees, item 5/1.)

Reasoning (App. B, p. 96): IIFA Resolution 51 permits it if agreed at contracting; no text forbids it; it serves a lawful interest. Ibn 'Abidin (Hanafi) notes that a creditor who gives up the deferral makes the debt due at once. Kuwait Finance House's Shari'ah board agreed (Fatwa 542).

Juristic logic. Acceleration changes the timing of the debt, not its amount. In practice, many SSCs require that the bank then gives up the unearned portion of the deferred profit (a rebate, ibra') when it collects early; SS 3 itself does not say this, so check SS 8 and your SSC's policy.

EXAMPLE

Karim paid 9 of 24 instalments and missed the 10th. Remaining instalments: 24 − 9 = 15. Under acceleration, 15 × BDT 50,000 = BDT 7,50,000 becomes due now, after a notice and, say, 15 days' grace. The total stays BDT 7,50,000; it does not grow.

NON-COMPLIANCE

Accelerating when a cyclone destroyed the customer's shop (force majeure), or adding a "breakage fee" on top of the accelerated amount.

4.3 Repossessing a Murabahah asset on bankruptcy

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/7 · p. 89

In a Murabahah sale, if the sold asset is still available in the condition in which it was sold, and the buyer defaulted and later became bankrupt, the seller (the IFI) may take the asset back instead of going through bankruptcy proceedings.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 97): Evidence 7 (Bukhari 2402). App. B extends it to "Murabahah or another sales contract".

Juristic logic. This is the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali position; the Hanafis disagree and treat the seller as an ordinary creditor. Note the interesting overlap: this clause concerns a bankrupt buyer, even though SS 3's scope excludes the insolvent. It applies because the default began while the buyer was still procrastinating.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · PRACTICE

Whether a Bangladeshi court would enforce this priority over other creditors depends on national insolvency law, which follows English-law principles. The bank should take a registered charge on the asset rather than rely on the hadith-based priority alone.

4.4 The charity undertaking

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/1/8 · p. 89

In debt contracts such as Murabahah, the debtor may undertake that if he procrastinates he will donate an amount or a percentage of the debt, to be spent on charitable causes through the Institution.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 97): this is a binding commitment to donate (iltizam bi al-tabarru'), well known in the Maliki school; App. B names Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar and cites al-Hattab's Tahrir al-Kalam fi Masa'il al-Iltizam.

Juristic logic. The money never becomes the creditor's. So it gives the debtor a reason to pay on time without being riba. Its legitimacy depends entirely on where the money goes.

Figure 4. Where the charity money must flow.

EXAMPLE

The Murabahah contract states: "If I delay any instalment without valid reason, I undertake to donate BDT 1,000 per delayed instalment to charitable causes through the bank." Karim delays 3 instalments: he donates BDT 3,000 (3 × 1,000), credited to the bank's charity account and paid out under SSC supervision. The bank's profit is unchanged.

NON-COMPLIANCE
  • Booking the donation as income, or using it to offset provisions, staff costs or write-offs.
  • Paying it to the bank's own foundation for publicity that benefits the bank (many SSCs forbid this; see Masum & Islam 2022 on Bangladeshi "compensation funds").
  • Charging it to a customer who proved genuine hardship.
  • Making the donation grow day by day exactly like interest. SS 3 allows "an amount or a percentage", but regulators increasingly prefer a fixed sum (see BB 2026, Chapter 7).
বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

চুক্তির সময় গ্রাহক অঙ্গীকার করেন যে, তিনি বিনা কারণে দেরি করলে নির্দিষ্ট পরিমাণ টাকা দান করবেন। এই টাকা ব্যাংক গ্রাহকের প্রতিনিধি হিসেবে আলাদা "চ্যারিটি অ্যাকাউন্টে" রাখে এবং শরিয়াহ কমিটির তত্ত্বাবধানে দাতব্য কাজে ব্যয় করে। এটি কখনোই ব্যাংকের আয় হবে না। বাংলাদেশে অনেক ব্যাংক একে "কমপেনসেশন" বলে, কিন্তু নাম যাই হোক, মূল বিষয় হলো অর্থটি কোথায় যাচ্ছে।

4.5 Set-off from the customer's accounts

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/5/3 · p. 90

A debt contract may stipulate that if the debtor is late, the IFI may recover the amount from any of his accounts with it, current or investment, without further consent, if the account is in the same currency as the debt. If the currency differs, the prevailing exchange rate on the day must be used.

STUDY TIP

Set-off: same currency: direct; different currency: today's rate. No consent needed if stipulated.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 100): the condition is binding (Evidence 5) and rests on the right of recovery (Evidence 10). App. B says the right exists even without consent, but it is better to write it into the contract to avoid disputes.

Juristic logic. For a current account the bank is the debtor (a loan from the customer), so the two debts cancel. For a Mudarabah investment account the customer owns a share of a pool, so the bank must first redeem it at its actual value, including any loss, before setting off.

EXAMPLE

Karim owes BDT 1,50,000. He has BDT 80,000 in a Mudarabah savings account and USD 500 in a foreign currency account. Rate on the day: BDT 122 per USD. Set-off: 80,000 + (500 × 122 = 61,000) = BDT 1,41,000. Remaining debt: 1,50,000 − 1,41,000 = BDT 9,000. Using an old, more favourable rate (say BDT 125) would be non-compliant.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH

See AAOIFI SS 4 (Settlement of Debts by Set-Off) for the full rules. The SBP adopted SS 4 in 2024 (IFPD Circular 01 of 2024).

5. Guarantor and contractor

অধ্যায় ৫: জামিনদার ও ঠিকাদার (২/২, ২/৩)

5.1 The guarantor

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/2 · p. 89

(a) The creditor may demand payment from either the debtor or the guarantor, unless the guarantor stipulated that the debtor must be asked first. (b) All rulings on defaulting debtors apply equally to defaulting guarantors.

Reasoning (App. B, pp. 97–98): suretyship joins one liability to another (Evidence 8). A stipulated sequence is valid because "believers are bound by their conditions".

Juristic logic. This follows the majority view that the creditor can claim from either party. Because 2/2(b) applies all of SS 3 to the guarantor, a guarantor who can pay but stalls is also sinning, may also be blacklisted, and also may not be charged compensation for delay.

Figure 5. Claiming from debtor or guarantor (2/2 a).

EXAMPLE

Rahim guarantees his brother's BDT 5 lakh Bai-Muajjal. The brother misses BDT 60,000. Unless Rahim's guarantee said "claim from my brother first", the bank may ask Rahim directly for BDT 60,000. If Rahim, who is well-off, then stalls, the bank may apply SS 3 tools to Rahim, but may not charge him a late fee for its own income.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

জামিনদারের দায় মূল দেনাদারের দায়ের সাথে যুক্ত হয়। ব্যাংক চাইলে যেকোনো একজনের কাছে পাওনা চাইতে পারে, যদি না জামিনদার আগে থেকে শর্ত দিয়ে থাকেন যে প্রথমে দেনাদারের কাছে চাইতে হবে। জামিনদার সামর্থ্য থাকা সত্ত্বেও দেরি করলে তাঁর ক্ষেত্রেও একই বিধান।

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH

The detailed law of guarantees is in AAOIFI SS 5 (Guarantees), which SS 3 cross-refers to at 2/1/6. The SBP compendium includes SS 5 with its own amendments.

5.2 The contractor and the penalty clause

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/3 · p. 89

Penalty clauses may be included in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts. If the contractor refuses to pay the penalty, the rules on debtor default apply to that amount. The penalty may be deducted from amounts owed to the contractor.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 98): such a clause does not make the unlawful lawful (Evidence 5); Qadi Shurayh held that whoever binds himself to a condition freely is bound by it; IIFA's Istisna'a resolution allows penalty clauses; the Hanbali school and Saudi Arabia's Council of Senior Scholars accept them. App. B ends with the key limit: penalty clauses are allowed only for non-financial obligations.

Juristic logic. Building a road or delivering goods is work, not a debt. Compensating for late work does not sell time on money. But once the penalty amount is due, it becomes a debt, and no further penalty may be charged on that amount. This is why 2/3 says the debtor-default rules then apply.

Figure 6. The dividing line for penalty clauses (SS 3 2/3; IIFA 109).

EXAMPLE · PARALLEL ISTISNA'A

An Islamic bank orders a garment factory building from a contractor under parallel Istisna'a, price BDT 5 crore, with a penalty of BDT 50,000 per week of late handover. The contractor is 6 weeks late. Penalty: 6 × 50,000 = BDT 3,00,000, deducted from the final payment due to the contractor.

On the other side, the bank's customer owes the bank the Istisna'a price. If the customer pays late, the bank may not charge a penalty for its income, because that is a debt.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · IIFA 109

IIFA Resolution 109 (3/12) (Riyadh, September 2000) allows penalty clauses in all financial contracts except where the original obligation is a debt, which would be clear riba. It gives construction, supply and the Istisna'a manufacturer as permitted cases, and the instalment-sale debtor and the Istisna'a purchaser as forbidden ones. It adds two limits SS 3 does not state: the clause lapses if the party proves the failure was beyond its control or that no loss occurred, and a court may adjust an excessive amount. Compensable loss covers actual loss and certain lost gain, not moral harm.

NON-COMPLIANCE

Charging a weekly penalty on a contractor's unpaid penalty balance; or inserting a "penalty clause" into a Murabahah because "it's just like a construction contract".

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

নির্মাণ, ইস্তিসনা ও সরবরাহ চুক্তিতে কাজ দেরিতে হলে জরিমানার শর্ত রাখা জায়েজ, কারণ এখানে দেরি হচ্ছে কাজে, টাকায় নয়। কিন্তু যেখানে দায়টি নিজেই দেনা (যেমন মুরাবাহার মূল্য), সেখানে জরিমানা নেওয়া সুদ।

জরিমানার টাকা ঠিকাদারের পাওনা থেকে কেটে রাখা যাবে।

6. Non-material sanctions and general rulings

অধ্যায় ৬: অ-আর্থিক শাস্তি ও সাধারণ বিধান (২/৪, ২/৫)

6.1 Blacklisting and warning others

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/4 · p. 90

The IFI may put a defaulting debtor's name on a list of undesirable customers (a black list) and warn other companies about him, either when they ask or when such lists are exchanged between companies.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 99): Evidence 2 makes the procrastinator's honour open to complaint. Telling others is not forbidden backbiting; it is a duty of sincere advice (nasihah).

Juristic logic. The sanction must be true (only real procrastinators, not the insolvent) and proportionate (shared with those who have a legitimate need). Public shaming beyond that is not covered.

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH · BANGLADESH

In Bangladesh this function is largely carried out through mandatory reporting to Bangladesh Bank's Credit Information Bureau (CIB). The 2026 Islamic credit card guideline requires CIB reporting of overdue accounts, bars harassment or threats, and limits recovery calls and visits to office hours. These limits fit the Shari'ah idea that the sanction must not exceed what is needed.

NON-COMPLIANCE

Posting a defaulter's photo on social media; calling his relatives and employer; listing a customer who has proved insolvency.

6.2 Monitoring the defaulter

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/5/1 · p. 90

The IFI may monitor and investigate the financial position and activities of a defaulting debtor by all lawful means.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 99): jurists recognise "pursuit" of the defaulter to find hidden assets; in these circumstances it is not prying into others' affairs. The square brackets in the clause text, "[monitor and]" and "[the financial status and activities]", appear to mark words added in the 2014 revision.

6.3 Accepting a voluntary extra payment

ORIGINAL STANDARD SS 3 · 2/5/2 · p. 90

The IFI may accept an amount above the debt from a defaulting debtor, provided there is no written or verbal condition, no custom and no mutual understanding about it.

Reasoning (App. B, p. 99): this is good repayment (Evidence 9). It must be entirely at the debtor's discretion; if it becomes a custom, it is no longer discretionary and is not allowed.

EXAMPLE

A customer who was late on his own initiative pays BDT 1,52,000 against BDT 1,50,000, saying "keep the extra, sorry for the trouble". The bank may accept the BDT 2,000. But if branch staff routinely tell late payers "customers usually add a little extra", a custom has formed and the extra becomes impermissible.

STUDY TIP

For 2/5/2 remember "No C-V-C-A": no Condition, no Verbal promise, no Custom, no Agreement.

বাংলা ব্যাখ্যা

দেনাদার যদি সম্পূর্ণ স্বেচ্ছায়, কোনো শর্ত বা প্রথা ছাড়াই কিছু বেশি দেন, ব্যাংক তা গ্রহণ করতে পারে। কিন্তু এটি যদি অলিখিত নিয়মে পরিণত হয়, তবে তা আর বৈধ থাকে না। আর খেলাপিকে কালো তালিকাভুক্ত করা যাবে, তবে কেবল প্রকৃত টালবাহানাকারীকে এবং যাদের জানা প্রয়োজন তাদের কাছে।

7.1 IIFA — the strictest on the principle, silent on charity

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH
  • Res. 51 (2/6), Jeddah, 14–20 March 1990: no increase for late instalments, agreed or not; no compensation even from a solvent delayer; acceleration allowed if agreed; seller cannot keep title but may take a mortgage on the sold item.
  • Res. 109 (3/12), Riyadh, 23–28 September 2000: penalty clauses valid except on debts.
  • Res. 133 (7/14), Doha, January 2003: reaffirms both; asks IFIs to study causes of arrears, obtain adequate guarantees and develop new recovery mechanisms. It does not mention the charity undertaking, set-off or blacklisting.

Practical meaning: IIFA supports SS 3's prohibitions but does not itself endorse SS 3's charity tool. That tool rests on the Maliki opinion that AAOIFI adopted.

7.2 Bangladesh Bank

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH
  • Guidelines for Conducting Islamic Banking (BB circular of 9 November 2009) define "compensation" as a financial penalty above the instalment when a client fails to repay on time. Masum and Islam (2022, Islamic Economic Studies) point out a gap: Bangladeshi banks actually treat these amounts as donations kept in a "compensation fund" spent on charity, yet the guideline calls them compensation. They also note that Bangladesh has no full Islamic Banking Act.
  • Bank schedules of charges show the mix. Jamuna Bank's Islami banking schedule says compensation may be charged for the overdue period and spent on charitable causes, and that charging it is discouraged. Eastern Bank's July 2026 Islamic corporate schedule lists "compensation for Murabahah-based financing, if applied" at an additional 1.5% of the overdue amount. The schedule does not say where this goes; a student should ask whether it is income or charity.
  • Guidelines on Islamic Credit Card Operations (IBRPD Circular 01, 27 September 2026): the cardholder gives an undertaking at contracting to donate a fixed amount on late payment; it is not bank income; it goes to a segregated Charity Account; the SSC approves the structure and verifies disbursement; it may be charged once per payment period; it may be charged on rescheduled accounts only if the cardholder is solvent; collection costs are recoverable only as actually paid to external agents. This is the closest BB rule to SS 3 2/1/8 and 2/1/4, even though AAOIFI is not named.
  • Governance context: an Islamic Banking Regulation and Policy Department (IBRPD) was set up in 2025; mandatory SSCs and a BB Shari'ah Advisory Board were introduced in 2025.

7.3 State Bank of Pakistan

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH

SBP adopted SS 3 under the title "Default in Payment by a Debtor" by IBD Circular No. 01 of 2010 (12 January 2010). Its only amendment adds "on giving the debtor reasonable notice of sale" to the collateral-sale sub-clause (2/1/5), so the bank must notify before using its mandate. All SBP amendments are consolidated in the Compendium of Shariah Standards (updated to 31 July 2025).

7.4 Bank Negara Malaysia

ADDITIONAL RESEARCH

BNM's Shariah Advisory Council took a different path (SAC resolutions):

  • 95th meeting (28 January 2010): ta'widh (compensation) may be charged for late payment in exchange contracts and qard, after the agreed payment period; it may be recognised as income because it covers actual loss; BNM sets the rate.
  • 101st meeting (20 May 2010): a late payment charge may combine gharamah (penalty) and ta'widh; the gharamah part may not be income and must go to charity; the customer's ability to pay must be considered; BNM sets maximum rates.

In practice, Malaysian banks publish ta'widh at actual cost up to 1% p.a. on overdue instalments during the tenor, and up to the Islamic interbank rate after maturity (for example Alliance Islamic Bank's fee page).

WHY AAOIFI WOULD NOT ACCEPT BNM'S TA'WIDH

Under SS 3 2/1/2, compensation for opportunity loss is forbidden even if it is "actual". A rate linked to an interbank money market rate looks, in substance, like a time-value charge on a debt. Supporters reply that it is capped, compensates real loss and applies only to the wilful. This is a genuine difference of juristic opinion between regulators, not a factual dispute.

STUDY TIP

One line each: AAOIFI – charity only; IIFA – no increase, full stop; BB – charity, fixed, segregated (cards); SBP – SS 3 + notice of sale; BNM – ta'widh to income, gharamah to charity.

8. Case studies and common misconceptions

অধ্যায় ৮: কেস স্টাডি ও প্রচলিত ভুল ধারণা

Case 1 · The busy importer

FACTS

Nasir Enterprises has a Murabahah of BDT 60 lakh, 12 monthly instalments of BDT 5 lakh. After paying 4, it stops paying. Its bank statements show BDT 1.2 crore of sales in the same period. Two demand letters are ignored.

Analysis. Due + demand + no proof of hardship: default is established (2/6), and the delay is haram (2/1/1). The bank may: invoke acceleration of the remaining 8 instalments, 8 × 5 lakh = BDT 40 lakh (2/1/6), after notice; collect the agreed charity amount into its charity account (2/1/8); set off any balances (2/5/3); recover actual legal costs (2/1/4); report to CIB (2/4). It may not add any amount to its income for the delay (2/1/2).

Case 2 · The flood-hit farmer

FACTS

A Bai-Muajjal agricultural investment customer in Sunamganj misses two instalments after flash floods wipe out his crop. He provides a union parishad certificate.

Analysis. He is insolvent for now and has a recognised excuse: outside SS 3 (clause 1). Qur'an 2:280 calls for grace. Acceleration is barred because the cause is force majeure (2/1/6). No charity undertaking should be enforced. Blacklisting him as a "procrastinator" would be untrue. The bank should reschedule without increasing the amount.

Case 3 · The late contractor

FACTS

Under a parallel Istisna'a, a contractor must deliver 20 houses by 30 June with a penalty of BDT 25,000 per house per month. He delivers 8 houses 2 months late.

Analysis. Work is a non-debt obligation, so the penalty is valid (2/3). Amount: 8 × 2 × 25,000 = BDT 4,00,000, deductible from the next payment to him. If he disputes it and the amount becomes a debt he refuses to pay, the bank may not add a further penalty on the BDT 4 lakh. Under IIFA 109, he can escape the penalty if he proves the delay was beyond his control.

Case 4 · The "processing fee" on rescheduling

FACTS

A bank reschedules an overdue BDT 10 lakh Bai-Muajjal over 12 more months and charges a "rescheduling processing fee" of 6% (BDT 60,000), booked as income.

Analysis. Substance over form. A fee that is proportional to the debt and paid for more time is riba (2/1/2), whatever its name. The bank may recover only its actual administrative costs of rescheduling, documented, not a percentage. A compliant restructure keeps the remaining price unchanged.

Case 5 · The guarantor with a sequence clause

FACTS

Fatema guaranteed her husband's Hire-Purchase-under-Shirkatul-Melk instalments. Her guarantee states "the bank shall first demand from the principal". Her husband misses BDT 40,000 and the bank immediately debits Fatema's savings account.

Analysis. The sequence condition is valid and binding (2/2 a). The bank must first demand from the husband. Debiting Fatema's account at once is non-compliant. Set-off against her account (2/5/3) is only possible once she herself owes and defaults, and only if her guarantee contains a set-off stipulation.

10. Answers with explanations

অধ্যায় ১০: উত্তরমালা ও ব্যাখ্যা

10.1 Conceptual answers

  1. Clause 1 excludes the insolvent because the Shari'ah requires that a debtor in hardship be given time: Qur'an 2:280. His delay is not zulm, since the hadith condemns delay by the ghani (person of means). Sanctions designed for wilful delay would be unjust against him.
  2. Compensation for delay is a payment for the time the creditor was kept out of its money (lost profit, cost of funds); it is riba (2/1/2). Expenses are actual sums the creditor paid because of the default, such as lawyer's and court fees; the debtor caused them, so he bears them (2/1/4). Test: would the amount exist if the creditor had spent nothing? If yes, it is compensation.
  3. A debt must be repaid in the same amount of the same currency. Topping it up for inflation or exchange-rate loss increases the debt in return for time, which is the same as riba. 2/1/2 closes this loophole explicitly.
  4. It is a binding commitment to make a gift (iltizam bi al-tabarru'), recognised by Maliki jurists such as Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar (App. B, p. 97). It is legitimate only because the money goes to charity through the IFI and never benefits the creditor.
  5. In construction the delayed obligation is work, a non-financial obligation; a penalty compensates for late performance, not time on money. In Murabahah the delayed obligation is the price, a debt; any penalty is an increase on a debt for time = riba (App. B, p. 98; IIFA 109).
  6. (i) The debt is due; (ii) a normal demand has been made; (iii) the debtor has not proved insolvency (2/6).
  7. SBP adds "on giving the debtor reasonable notice of sale". So a Pakistani IFI cannot use its mandate to sell collateral immediately; it must first notify the debtor and allow reasonable time, which gives the debtor a last chance to pay.
  8. AAOIFI SS 3 is a standard: no compensation of any kind kept by the creditor; only charity. BNM's SAC ruling, enforced by BNM, is regulation based on a juristic opinion: ta'widh for actual loss may be income, gharamah goes to charity, both capped. The disagreement is juristic, about whether "actual loss" compensation is riba.

11.1 Revision notes

  • Scope: solvent debtor, solvent guarantor, late contractor. Excludes insolvent/bankrupt and valid excuse.
  • Ruling: procrastination by the able = haram (Bukhari 2287).
  • Two nos: no contractual compensation (cash/kind, fixed or not, opportunity or currency loss); no court claim.
  • Costs: actual legal and recovery expenses only.
  • Collateral: sale through court, or by mandate without court (SBP: plus reasonable notice).
  • Acceleration: allowed, except force majeure; notice and reasonable time preferable.
  • Repossession: Murabahah asset still as sold + buyer bankrupt (Bukhari 2402).
  • Charity undertaking: amount or % to charity through IFI; Maliki basis; never income.
  • Guarantor: claim either, unless sequence stipulated; same rules apply to him.
  • Contractor: penalty clause OK for construction, Istisna'a, supply; deductible; non-financial obligations only.
  • Non-material: blacklist and warn others (Abu Dawud 3628).
  • General: lawful investigation; voluntary extra OK without condition/custom; set-off from any account, same currency or prevailing rate.
  • Default established: due + normal demand + no proof of insolvency.
  • Dates: issued 27 Safar 1421 / 31 May 2000; revised version adopted June 2014 (meeting 38).

WHAT SS 3 FORBIDS
  • Stalling by a debtor who can pay (2/1/1)
  • Any late-payment compensation in the contract, cash or kind, fixed or not, opportunity or currency loss (2/1/2)
  • Court claims for delay compensation (2/1/3)

FIVE PROOFS TO MEMORISE
  • Bukhari 2287 — delay by the rich is injustice
  • Abu Dawud 3628 — honour and punishment lawful
  • Qur'an 2:280 — grace for the one in hardship
  • Tirmidhi 1352 — bound by conditions, except…
  • Bukhari 2402 — seller finds goods with a bankrupt
WHAT SS 3 ALLOWS
  • Actual legal/recovery costs (2/1/4)
  • Sale of collateral; mandate to sell (2/1/5)
  • Acceleration, except force majeure (2/1/6)
  • Repossession on bankruptcy (2/1/7)

THREE TESTS
  1. Is the late obligation a debt? Yes: no penalty for creditor.
  2. Who keeps the money? Creditor: riba; charity: may be valid.
  3. Is the debtor able? No: grace, outside SS 3.
